purpose: Run a matched SQLite backup/restore comparison between restic and Litestream against a copy of the ai-memory store, and a matched Python SDK-graph install comparison between uv and mise, both installed pinned into fresh prefixes, to produce a first executed measurement for open_gaps[8] ('No measured comparison exists between Restic and Litestream, or between uv and mise') and open_gaps[14] ('No executed comparison establishes that an alternative improves installation or recovery').
preregistered: SQLite arm: back up and restore one checkpointed, single-file copy of the live ai-memory SQLite store (never the live store itself) with both restic and Litestream, recording exit codes, wall time, on-disk repository/replica size, and restore fidelity (sha256 byte-identity as the strict check, PRAGMA integrity_check plus matching pages/observations row counts as the logical-fidelity fallback if byte-identity fails). SDK arm: install the same 36-distribution hash-locked Python SDK graph with uv (`uv pip sync --require-hashes`, already measured in the sibling uv-fresh-cache-sdk-graph-sync.json receipt) and with mise (provision the pinned CPython via `mise use`, then install the same lock with the mise-provisioned interpreter's pip, since mise itself has no native hash-locked Python dependency resolver), recording exit codes, wall time and resolved distribution counts for both. If either alternative (Litestream, mise) matches or beats the incumbent (restic, uv) on time and fidelity for this workload, that would refute restic/uv's advantage on this specific measured axis; if it does not, or has a structural capability gap (e.g. mise cannot itself resolve a hash-locked graph), that supports the incumbent choice. Any nonzero exit code on either side is recorded as a failure, not smoothed over.

correction_2026-09-23.finding: A fix-round review found the original `result` explained the SQLite-arm byte-level divergence wrongly and overstated restore fidelity. The original text said the change was 'consistent with SQLite incrementing header change-counter ... independent of any logical write' and that 'logical/row-level content stayed correct'. The fidelity check counted only pages/observations rows, which cannot detect a schema difference. In fact Litestream adds its own tracking tables (`_litestream_seq`, `_litestream_lock`) to the schema of any database it replicates -- both the monitored source copy and the restored replica -- while the restic restore has neither table. This is a schema-level difference the original fidelity check never looked for, not merely a header-field/change-counter artifact.
correction_2026-09-23.settled_by: A read-only sqlite_master table-name lookup on the exact three files the original receipt already produced (no new backup/restore run needed): aim-store-copy/memory.sqlite (the litestream-monitored source, post-run, sha256 dcc06fa3... as originally recorded), backup-compare/litestream-restore.sqlite (same sha256), and the restic restore's memory.sqlite. Helper: blueprints/gap-wave2-20260923/restic-vs-litestream-uv-vs-mise/schema_diff.py.

correction_2026-09-23.preregistration_for_this_check: If both the litestream-monitored source copy and the litestream restore contain `_litestream_seq`/`_litestream_lock` tables that the restic restore does not, that confirms Litestream's own control-table schema addition (not a bare change-counter increment) explains the byte divergence, and the restored database is not logically/schematically identical to the pre-replication source -- refuting the original receipt's 'logical/row-level content stayed correct' claim (row counts matched, but the schema did not). If instead all three files have identical table sets, the original change-counter explanation would need to stand and this correction would be void.
correction_2026-09-23.result: Confirmed: `select name from sqlite_master where type='table'` on all three files shows aim-store-copy/memory.sqlite and backup-compare/litestream-restore.sqlite each contain `_litestream_lock` and `_litestream_seq` (57 tables total) while the restic restore's memory.sqlite has neither (55 tables, otherwise identical table names). Output sha256: c69f4c9f4a2e13af9182231e6dfcd9e47e9e0e0af2042e275c4b59547e4b1424 (full table lists in that file, kept outside the repo per the raw-artifact size threshold even though small, alongside this unit's other scratch state).
correction_2026-09-23.corrected_conclusion: The byte-level divergence is explained by Litestream writing its own two tracking tables into the schema of the file it opens/monitors (observed here on the monitored source copy itself, before any restore), which the restic-based comparison never does. The original 'logical/row-level content stayed correct' claim is corrected: application table row counts (pages/observations) matched, but the restored database's schema is not identical to the pre-replication source -- a real, additional (not merely change-counter-level) fidelity gap for Litestream on this workload, on top of (not instead of) the byte-identity/mutation finding the original receipt already reported correctly.

result: CORRECTED 2026-09-23 (see correction_2026-09-23 above). SQLite arm: restic backed up the 214MB checkpointed store copy in 1.42s and restored it in 1.15s, producing a byte-for-byte identical file (sha256 match) and never touching the source file's bytes. Litestream's one-shot snapshot replication took 2.47s and its restore took 1.65s (both slower than restic's equivalent step), produced a file with the same size, PRAGMA integrity_check=ok, and identical pages/observations row counts (405 / 155159) as the source -- but NOT a byte-identical file versus the pre-replication source hash, AND (per the fix-round correction) not a schema-identical one either: the restored database contains two extra tables, `_litestream_lock` and `_litestream_seq`, that the pre-replication source and the restic restore do not have. Investigating the byte discrepancy: re-hashing the source file after the Litestream run showed the SOURCE ITSELF had changed to match the Litestream restore's hash, diverging from its own pre-replication hash that restic's restore still matches. A read-only sqlite_master lookup (the correction) shows this is because Litestream's replicate step writes its own control tables into the schema of the file it opens/monitors, not (or not only) a bare SQLite header change-counter increment as originally guessed -- a real, measured, operationally significant difference: restic's backup is purely read-only against its source, while Litestream's replication is not, and it also alters the monitored/restored database's schema. On-disk repository/replica size: restic's repo was 62MB (compressed, ~29% of source) vs Litestream's replica at 232MB (LTX format, close to full source size, no compression observed at this pin/config). SDK arm: uv's hash-locked sync (measured in the sibling receipt) resolved+installed 36 distributions in 3.32s with a fresh empty cache; mise itself has no native hash-locked Python dependency resolver, so the fairest matched equivalent is mise provisioning the pinned CPython 3.13.15 interpreter (2.9s) and then using that interpreter's bundled pip to install the identical lock file (13.1s, `--require-hashes`, `--no-cache-dir`), which also succeeded (exit 0) and resolved the same 36 named distributions by name+version. Combined interpreter-provision-plus-install time for the mise/pip path (~16s) was roughly 4-5x slower than uv's single-step sync (3.3s) on this workload.

verdict_impact.explanation: This is the first executed, matched comparison for both pairs (previously source-review only), directly answering open_gaps[8] and materially informing open_gaps[14]. On this workload, restic was faster on both backup and restore, produced a smaller (compressed) repository, and -- most importantly -- left the source database byte- and schema-unmodified, while Litestream was slower, mutated the monitored source file's bytes as an inherent side effect of replication, and (per the fix-round correction) also added its own control tables (`_litestream_lock`, `_litestream_seq`) to the schema of both the monitored source and the restored replica -- application-level row counts matched, but the schema itself did not, which is a stronger drawback than the originally-reported byte-only divergence. uv was faster than a mise-provisioned-interpreter-plus-pip path and, unlike mise, has a native hash-locked resolver for this exact lock format; mise's role is toolchain/interpreter provisioning, not Python dependency-graph resolution, which is a structural capability gap rather than a performance-tuning difference. Neither alternative outperformed the incumbent on this workload, so this does not change either verdict, but it replaces an unexecuted assumption with a concrete measurement, which is what open_gaps[8] asked for.

limitations: Single run per tool per arm, no retry-to-fish per the preregistration rule; timing reflects one measurement on a shared host, not a statistically averaged benchmark.

The SQLite arm used one checkpointed static copy of the ai-memory store, not a live, continuously-written database under concurrent load -- Litestream's actual design point (continuous WAL-tailing replication of an actively written database) was not exercised; this comparison measures a one-shot snapshot backup/restore, which favors restic's simpler file-copy model and may understate Litestream's value for its intended continuous-replication use case.

The source-file-mutation finding (Litestream changing the monitored file's bytes on open) was diagnosed from indirect evidence (before/after sha256 of the source plus Litestream's own log and the appearance of a new .memory.sqlite-litestream sidecar directory next to the source), not from an isolated single-variable experiment separating 'opening a WAL-mode SQLite connection' from 'Litestream specifically'; the SQLite copy already had journal_mode=WAL set by this check's own checkpoint step before Litestream touched it, so the observed byte change could also partly reflect ordinary WAL-mode connection-open semantics rather than a Litestream-specific behavior. A fix-round correction (correction_2026-09-23) settled the schema portion of this question with a direct sqlite_master lookup (Litestream demonstrably adds its own `_litestream_lock`/`_litestream_seq` tables, which plain WAL-mode connection-open does not do), but did not run an isolated single-variable experiment for the remaining byte-level (non-schema) portion of the divergence, so that narrower question is still open.

The uv-vs-mise SDK-graph comparison is not perfectly matched: uv performs its own dependency resolution against a pre-computed lock in one step, while the mise arm uses mise only for interpreter provisioning and delegates package installation to a separate tool (pip) that mise does not itself provide a hash-locked-resolution wrapper for; this asymmetry is itself part of the answer to open_gaps[8]/[14] (a structural, not merely performance, difference) but means the two numbers are not a pure apples-to-apples resolver benchmark.
Both alternative prefixes (litestream-0.5.17-w2, mise-2026.9.12-w2) and all scratch artifacts remain under the session state directory, not the repository, per the raw-artifact size threshold.
Litestream's replica directory (232MB) and the mise pip-venv (part of the 727MB mise-w2 scratch tree) were left on disk as durable evidence, not cleaned up, consistent with this unit's other checks.
